どんな まち です か — What’s the town like?
You describe things, people and places with adjectives: those ending in -い and those with な, in the affirmative, the negative and the past.
What kind of city is Kyoto?
To tell -い adjectives (おおきい) from な adjectives (きれい).
To put them before a noun: おおきい まち, きれい な まち.
To use them in the negative: おおきくない / きれい じゃ ありません.
To use them in the past: さむかった / しずか でした.
To ask どう (how?) and どんな (what kind of?) and to link two adjectives (～くて / ～で).
Mrs Tanaka has gone home and sent photos of Kyoto. Yuki shows them to Mihai on her phone, at the library.
Mihai, look. These are Mum’s photos.
Wow, how beautiful! Where is this?
It’s Kyoto. Kyoto is an old, quiet city.
It’s a Japanese maple. The autumn maples are very famous.
And this big building? Is it a temple?
Yes, it’s Kiyomizu temple. It’s about a thousand years old.
Amazing! Is Kyoto a lively city?
It’s lively near the station. But around the temples it isn’t very busy.
In the morning it was cold. But at midday it was warm and lovely.
In autumn they’re expensive. But the traditional inn was very good. And the people were kind.
One day, I want to go to Kyoto too.
Then let’s go together next summer! But it’s very hot in summer, you know.
(links a な adjective to a noun)
Adjectives often end in a long -ii: o-o-ki-i. Hold the last “i” for a whole beat, or おおきい becomes a mistake.
The u in “mu” almost disappears: “m’zukashii”. Japanese people say “muzukashii” quickly.
ゆう = “yuu” (long u). めい and れい are read “meh”, “reh”: yuu-meh, ki-reh.
Japanese has two kinds of adjectives. You need to know which family each one belongs to, because they behave differently:
Trap! きれい and ゆうめい end in -い, but they’re な adjectives. Learn them as exceptions. The app’s dictionary writes “(な)” next to them.
As in English, the adjective comes BEFORE: “big city” = おおきい まち. な adjectives take な in the middle:
At the end of a sentence, both go with です, without な: まち は おおきい です / まち は しずか です.
たかい → たかくない です (it isn’t expensive)
The most important exception: いい (good) → よくない です (it isn’t good). There’s no “いくない”!
A more polite version for -い: たかく ありません. Both are correct.
さむかった です (it was cold)
さむくなかった です (it wasn’t cold)
しずか でした (it was quiet)
The typical mistake: “さむい でした”. Wrong! With -い adjectives, the past is in the adjective itself: さむかった です. Only な adjectives use でした.
5. How? What kind of? And two adjectives at once
To link two adjectives (“old AND quiet”):
ふるくて、しずか です (old and quiet)
しずか で、きれい です (quiet and beautiful)
“But” between two sentences: ～が. にほんご は むずかしい です が、おもしろい です (Japanese is difficult, but interesting).
Which one is a な adjective?
Kyoto is an old, quiet city.
What were the people at the inn like?
マドリード と とうきょう — Madrid and Tokyo
Yuki compares the two cities in an essay for Ana’s Spanish class, but first she writes it in Japanese.
Tokyo is a very big city. There are a great many people.
Madrid is smaller than Tokyo, but it’s lively.
Tokyo’s trains are fast and convenient. But in the morning they’re very crowded.
The Madrid metro isn’t very new, but it’s clean.
In Madrid it’s hot in summer and cold in winter. The sky is always blue.
In Tokyo it’s hot in summer, but it rains a lot.
Spaniards are cheerful and kind. And there’s life in the streets at night.
Japanese people are quiet, but very gentle.
What’s the difference between the summers in the two cities?
It rains a lot in Tokyo
It rains a lot in Madrid
How does Yuki describe Japanese people?
あたらしい へや — The new flat
Mihai’s flat is old and small.
The window is small too, and in winter it’s very cold.
On top of that, the neighbour sings every evening. It’s not quiet at all!
So Mihai is looking for a new flat.
On Saturday, Mihai and Ana went to the estate agent’s.
The man at the agency was very kind. He showed them three flats.
The first flat is in the city centre.
It was new, spacious and very beautiful.
But outside it’s hectic, and at night it’s noisy too. And it’s very expensive.
“It’s a good flat, but it’s a bit…,” said Mihai.
But it was far from the station and not very convenient.
The room was dark and a bit dirty. And the kitchen was old.
The third flat is next to a park.
It isn’t very new. But it’s bright and quiet.
The windows are big, and from the window you can see the trees in the park.
It’s ten minutes’ walk to the hospital. And the rent isn’t high either.
At that moment, a small voice came from behind the door. “Miaow.”
Behind the door was a white kitten.
“Ah! This cat is one of Tama’s kittens!” said Ana.
The man from the agency laughed. “Yes, it belongs to the old lady in this building.”
The old lady was the one from the library reception!
Mihai made up his mind straight away. “I’ll take this flat!”
Next month, Mihai is moving into the new flat.
He no longer has a neighbour who sings. But sometimes he hears a “miaow”.
The next day, Mihai called Kenji. “The new flat is spacious and quiet. Come and visit next time.”
“koe ga shimashita” = a voice was heard
Why does Mihai want a new flat?
It’s old, small, cold and noisy
What was the problem with the second flat?
Far from the station, dark, dirty
